concept.name: Serverless & FaaS Design

relationships.description: Connects Serverless & FaaS Design to system design hld architectures in the broader engineering catalog.

spark.summary: Serverless Function-as-a-Service (FaaS) executes stateless, event-driven handlers in ephemeral sandboxes—such as Firecracker microVMs (AWS Lambda) or V8 isolates (Cloudflare Workers)—scaling from zero to thousands of concurrent instances per second with per-millisecond billing. Designing for FaaS requires bounding cold starts, decoupling slow downstream dependencies via queues, and preventing connection-pool exhaustion.
spark.keyTakeaway: Design FaaS handlers to be small, idempotent, and stateless—offloading DB connection pooling to proxies and long workflows to async queues.

concept.whyItMatters: Traditional always-on VMs waste 60–80% of provisioned capacity during off-peak hours and require manual capacity planning for bursty workloads. FaaS eliminates idle compute billing and scales automatically to handle 10x traffic spikes in seconds. However, naive lift-and-shift designs fail catastrophically in serverless: 2,000 concurrent Lambda invocations opening direct PostgreSQL connections will exhaust `max_connections` in seconds, while bloated 200 MB Java/Python bundles trigger 3–8 second cold starts that breach API p99 SLOs.
whenToUse: Spiky, unpredictable, or intermittent workloads (webhooks, image/video thumbnailing, cron ETL jobs) where idle VMs would sit unused.
Event-driven glue pipelines reacting to S3 object uploads, Kafka/SQS messages, or CDC streams with independent per-message scaling.
Edge routing, auth token verification, and lightweight API BFFs running on sub-5 ms V8 isolates.
whenNotToUse: Long-running stateful workloads, WebSocket brokers, or ML training jobs exceeding platform limits (e.g., AWS Lambda's 15-minute max timeout and 10 GB RAM cap).
Sustained, flat, high-throughput compute (e.g., >70% constant CPU utilization 24/7), where FaaS per-GB-second pricing costs 2–4x more than reserved containers or EC2.
Ultra-low-latency trading or real-time game loops that cannot tolerate occasional tail cold starts or noisy-neighbor jitter.
keyPoints: Cold starts stem from sandbox boot + runtime init + dependency import: Firecracker microVMs add ~100–250 ms, whereas large JVM/Spring or Pandas bundles add 2–8 seconds.
Initialization outside the handler (`init` phase) runs once per execution environment and should host SDK clients, config, and compiled regexes—never per-request connections without reuse.
Stateless scale breaks stateful databases: always route relational DB traffic through RDS Proxy, PgBouncer, or HTTP-based serverless DB drivers.
At-least-once event delivery is the default for SQS, EventBridge, and DynamoDB Streams—handlers must enforce idempotency keys.
FaaS memory allocation scales CPU linearly (e.g., AWS Lambda gives 1 full vCPU at 1,769 MB): under-provisioning RAM to save pennies often slows execution and increases total GB-second cost.

examples.title: E-Commerce Order Webhook & Invoice Pipeline
examples.scenario: Flash sales spike checkout traffic from 20 req/s to 4,500 req/s for 12 minutes, where synchronous PDF invoice generation and email dispatch previously timed out API servers.
examples.outcome: API Gateway enqueues order events directly into SQS; a 512 MB Node.js Lambda consumer with DynamoDB idempotency keys (`order_id`) and `ReservedConcurrency = 150` processes bursts cleanly without overwhelming the downstream SMTP or RDS instance.

examples.title: JVM Cold-Start Remediation with SnapStart
examples.scenario: A Java 21 Spring Boot Lambda serving loan-quote APIs suffered 4.8-second p99 cold starts, causing mobile client timeouts during morning traffic ramps.
examples.outcome: Enabling AWS Lambda SnapStart (Firecracker CRaC memory snapshots) and stripping unused Spring starters reduced p99 cold starts from 4.8 s to 380 ms with zero Provisioned Concurrency spend.

tradeOffs.factor: MicroVMs (AWS Lambda) vs V8 Isolates (Cloudflare Workers)
tradeOffs.pro: MicroVMs support arbitrary Linux binaries, Docker images up to 10 GB, and full Python/Java/Go runtimes.
tradeOffs.con: V8 isolates boot in <5 ms with virtually zero cold start, whereas microVMs incur 100 ms–3 s cold starts.

tradeOffs.pro: Provisioned Concurrency keeps pre-warmed sandboxes ready, eliminating cold starts for latency-critical p99 paths.
tradeOffs.con: Converts pure pay-per-use into a fixed hourly baseline bill, eroding serverless cost savings if over-provisioned.

tradeOffs.pro: Nano-functions isolate IAM permissions (least privilege) and deploy independently.
tradeOffs.con: Sprawl across 80+ tiny functions fragments observability, duplicates boilerplate, and multiplies cold-start surface area.

failureModes.name: Database Connection Exhaustion
failureModes.description: A traffic burst spawns 1,500 concurrent function instances, each opening a TCP/TLS PostgreSQL connection and crashing the database at `max_connections = 500`.
failureModes.mitigation: Use RDS Proxy or PgBouncer for connection multiplexing, cap function `ReservedConcurrency`, or switch to HTTP/Data-API drivers.

failureModes.name: Retry Storm / Poison-Pill Loop
failureModes.description: An unhandled exception on a malformed SQS/Kafka record triggers automatic platform retries, burning concurrency quota and delaying healthy messages.
failureModes.mitigation: Configure `maxReceiveCount` (e.g., 3) with a Dead-Letter Queue (DLQ), return `batchItemFailures` for partial batch success, and apply exponential backoff.

failureModes.name: Recursive Invocation Loop
failureModes.description: A Lambda triggered by an S3 `ObjectCreated` event writes a transformed file back into the same bucket/prefix, triggering itself infinitely.
failureModes.mitigation: Separate input and output prefixes/buckets, enforce S3 event suffix filters, and enable platform recursive-loop detection.

failureModes.name: Sync Timeout Cascade
failureModes.description: API Gateway (29 s hard timeout) calls a Lambda that waits on a slow 35 s third-party payment API, causing client retries and duplicate charges.
failureModes.mitigation: Enforce strict HTTP client timeouts (<10 s), return HTTP 202 Accepted for long tasks backed by Step Functions/SQS, and use idempotency keys.

commonMistakes: Placing FaaS functions inside a VPC unnecessarily on legacy setups or without sizing NAT Gateways and ENI limits for burst concurrency.
Opening and closing database or HTTP clients inside the handler body instead of reusing connections across warm invocations.
Leaving default 128 MB memory on CPU-bound tasks (like JSON parsing or image resizing), which throttles CPU to ~0.07 vCPU and triples duration.
Passing >256 KB payloads through async event buses instead of storing blobs in S3 and passing a presigned URL or S3 key.
Deploying a single shared `AdministratorAccess` IAM role across all functions instead of per-function least-privilege policies.

sections.content:
## Ephemeral, event-driven compute with scale-to-zero economics

Serverless FaaS decouples code execution from server lifecycle management. Instead of running persistent processes, you package a handler function and attach event triggers (HTTP, queues, object storage, schedules). The platform's control plane schedules each invocation onto an isolated sandbox—either a lightweight Firecracker microVM (AWS Lambda) or a V8 isolate (Cloudflare Workers)—spinning up additional instances per concurrent request and freezing or reaping idle sandboxes after 5–15 minutes.

## Anatomy of a cold start vs warm invocation

1. **Event Arrival & Routing:** An HTTP POST hits API Gateway, which asks the FaaS placement service for an available warm sandbox for `fn:checkout-v12`.
2. **Cold Path (Miss):** If none exist, the worker downloads the container/ZIP layer, boots a Firecracker microVM (~100 ms), starts the Python/Node/JVM runtime, and executes top-level `init` code (loading SDKs, reading Secrets Manager).
3. **Handler Invocation:** The runtime invokes `handler(event, context)` with a strict deadline (e.g., 15 s). Warm invocations skip step 2 and execute in <2 ms overhead.
4. **Pooled I/O:** The handler checks a DynamoDB `idempotency_key` table and writes the order via RDS Proxy, which multiplexes 500 Lambda connections onto 20 persistent Postgres sockets.
5. **Freeze & Reuse:** Once the response returns, the microVM is frozen in memory—preserving global SDK clients and `/tmp` scratch files for the next request.

sections.content:
## Where initialization latency actually goes

Cold starts have two distinct phases: **platform overhead** (downloading the artifact and booting the sandbox) and **runtime init** (starting the interpreter/VM and importing dependencies). While Go or Rust binaries initialize in 30–80 ms, Python with `boto3` + `pandas` or Java with reflection-heavy DI frameworks can spend 1.5–6.0 seconds in `init`. Keeping bundle sizes under 10 MB via tree-shaking (esbuild), lazy-loading rarely used SDKs, using ARM64 (Graviton2/3) for 20% better price-performance, and enabling SnapStart for JVM workloads directly attacks runtime init.

## Choosing between FaaS execution models

| Execution Model | Typical Cold Start | Max Duration | Package / Memory Ceiling | Ideal Workload |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **V8 Isolates (Cloudflare Workers)** | <5 ms | 30 s–5 min (CPU-time capped) | ~10 MB / 128 MB–1 GB | Edge auth, A/B routing, lightweight API proxies |
| **Firecracker MicroVM (AWS Lambda - Go/Node)** | 120–350 ms | 15 min | 250 MB ZIP / 10 GB OCI; 10 GB RAM | REST APIs, SQS workers, event-driven microservices |
| **Firecracker + SnapStart (Java 21)** | 250–500 ms | 15 min | 250 MB ZIP; 10 GB RAM | Enterprise JVM APIs needing low cold-start tail latency |
| **Serverless Containers (Cloud Run / Fargate)** | 1–4 s | 60 min+ (or unlimited) | Arbitrary OCI; 32 GB+ RAM | Heavy ML inference, FFmpeg, multi-connection WebSockets |

## Production failure patterns in serverless architectures

1. **Downstream Stampede:** Because FaaS scales faster than relational databases or legacy monoliths, an unthrottled SQS consumer can DDoS your own database. Always set `ReservedConcurrency` or SQS `MaximumConcurrency`.
2. **Frozen Background Threads:** When a handler returns, the sandbox is immediately frozen—background `setTimeout` callbacks or async telemetry flushes never finish until the next invocation (or are lost on reap). Always `await` telemetry/logs before returning.
3. **Partial Batch Failure Blindness:** Returning an error from a 10-message SQS batch replays all 10 messages, re-executing the 9 that already succeeded.

## Avoiding Lambda-calls-Lambda anti-patterns

Never have Function A synchronously invoke Function B and wait—you pay double GB-second billing while Function A sits idle, and double your timeout exposure. Instead, coordinate multi-step workflows (payment -> inventory -> shipping with saga compensation) using state machines like **AWS Step Functions** or **Temporal**, or choreograph via **EventBridge / SQS**. Keep each function focused on a single bounded step with explicit retry, backoff, and compensation handlers.

## Production FaaS design checklist

- [ ] **Initialize SDKs outside handler:** Reuse HTTP keep-alive and AWS/GCP clients across warm invocations.
- [ ] **Enforce idempotency:** Key every mutating handler on a deterministic `request_id` in DynamoDB/Redis with a TTL.
- [ ] **Protect databases:** Route SQL traffic through RDS Proxy/PgBouncer and set `ReservedConcurrency` caps.
- [ ] **Use partial batch responses:** Return `batchItemFailures` for SQS/Kinesis/DynamoDB Streams and wire a DLQ.
- [ ] **Right-size memory:** Benchmark 512 MB vs 1,769 MB (1 vCPU) to minimize total `duration * memory` cost.
- [ ] **Await all I/O:** Flush OpenTelemetry spans and structured JSON logs before the handler returns.

interviewProblems.title: Serverless & FaaS Design
interviewProblems.scenarioPrompt: Design a production system that depends on Serverless & FaaS Design. What invariants, failure modes, and observability do you require?
interviewProblems.sampleDefense: Start from invariants, choose the pattern that preserves them, and add metrics for the known failure modes.
commonPitfalls: Optimizing throughput before defining correctness boundaries.

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: Serverless Function-as-a-Service (FaaS) executes stateless, event-driven handlers in ephemeral sandboxes—such as Firecracker microVMs (AWS Lambda) or V8 isolates (Cloudflare Workers)—scaling from zero to thousands of concurrent instances per second with per-millisecond billing. Designing for FaaS requires bounding cold starts, decoupling slow downstream dependencies via queues, and preventing connection-pool exhaustion.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: RDS Proxy + DynamoDB applies the primary invariant and coordinates with SQS DLQ & CloudWatch.

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, SQS DLQ & CloudWatch experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Use RDS Proxy or PgBouncer for connection multiplexing, cap function `ReservedConcurrency`, or switch to HTTP/Data-API drivers.

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: Design FaaS handlers to be small, idempotent, and stateless—offloading DB connection pooling to proxies and long workflows to async queues.
Avoid trap: Placing FaaS functions inside a VPC unnecessarily on legacy setups or without sizing NAT Gateways and ENI limits for burst concurrency.
Avoid trap: Opening and closing database or HTTP clients inside the handler body instead of reusing connections across warm invocations.
When to reach for it: Spiky, unpredictable, or intermittent workloads (webhooks, image/video thumbnailing, cron ETL jobs) where idle VMs would sit unused.
When to reach for it: Event-driven glue pipelines reacting to S3 object uploads, Kafka/SQS messages, or CDC streams with independent per-message scaling.

putItTogether.title: Putting Serverless Faas Design Together
putItTogether.summary: Design FaaS handlers to be small, idempotent, and stateless—offloading DB connection pooling to proxies and long workflows to async queues.
steps: Establish baseline invariants for Serverless Faas Design before scaling.
Isolate hot paths with caching, backpressure, or partitioning.
Verify failure modes with synthetic load & chaos checks.
putItTogether.outcome: API Gateway enqueues order events directly into SQS; a 512 MB Node.js Lambda consumer with DynamoDB idempotency keys (`order_id`) and `ReservedConcurrency = 150` processes bursts cleanly without overwhelming the downstream SMTP or RDS instance.
